title: Gambling Affiliate Rules in Canada: The 2026 Standards
excerpt: Affiliate sites shape where Canadians gamble, and regulators have tightened the rules. Here is how gambling affiliate marketing works in Canada in 2026.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Most Canadians who sign up for an online casino or sportsbook arrive there through a third party. A review site, a comparison table, a YouTube channel, a tipster account. These are affiliates, and they are paid by operators for the players they send. Gambling affiliate marketing is one of the least visible parts of the industry and one of the most influential, because it shapes the choice set most players ever see.

Regulators have noticed. Over the past few years, oversight of affiliate conduct in Canada's regulated markets has tightened considerably, and the relationship between operators and the sites promoting them now carries formal compliance obligations. This piece explains how the model works, what the rules require in 2026, and what it all means for you as a reader.

How affiliate marketing actually works

An affiliate publishes content about gambling and links to operators. When a reader follows that link, registers and deposits, the affiliate earns money. The commercial arrangements fall into a few standard shapes.

  • Revenue share. The affiliate receives a percentage of the operator's net revenue from that player, often for the lifetime of the account. This aligns the affiliate with long-term player value.
  • Cost per acquisition. A flat fee per qualifying new depositor. Simpler, front-loaded, and less tied to what happens afterwards.
  • Hybrid. A smaller upfront fee plus ongoing revenue share.

The structure matters more than it might appear. Revenue share on net revenue means an affiliate earns most from players who lose the most, which is an obvious tension in a business that also claims to give impartial advice. Cost-per-acquisition deals remove the ongoing link but create pressure to maximise signup volume regardless of fit.

Neither model is inherently disqualifying. Affiliate funding is how essentially all free gambling comparison content gets made, including sites like this one. What separates a useful affiliate from a harmful one is whether the commercial arrangement is disclosed and whether it visibly distorts the editorial judgment. We set out our own approach on our about page.

Where the regulation sits in 2026

Canada does not have a single national gambling regulator. Responsibility sits with the provinces, which means affiliate rules differ depending on which market an operator is licensed in.

Ontario

Ontario's regulated market is the most developed and carries the most detailed affiliate requirements. The governing principle is straightforward: the licensed operator is responsible for the conduct of anyone marketing on its behalf. An operator cannot outsource a compliance breach to a third party and disclaim it.

In practice this has produced several concrete obligations. Operators must maintain records of their marketing affiliates. Affiliate content must comply with the same advertising standards the operator itself is bound by, which in Ontario includes significant restrictions on how bonuses and inducements may be promoted publicly. Material that would be prohibited in an operator's own advertising cannot be published by an affiliate on the operator's behalf either.

The effect has been consolidation. Compliance overhead favours larger, established affiliates with legal resources, and a number of smaller operators pulled back from affiliate channels rather than take on the monitoring burden. Readers in the province can see how the licensed market looks in practice in our Ontario casino apps guide.

Alberta

Alberta's move to an open, regulated iGaming market brought a second competitive province online, and its framework has drawn substantially on Ontario's experience, including the principle of operator responsibility for affiliate conduct. For affiliates, the practical consequence is that content targeting Alberta players now needs to account for a distinct regulatory environment rather than being treated as generic Canadian content. Our Alberta sports betting guide covers what the market looks like from a player's side.

Everywhere else

Outside the competitive provinces, provincial lottery corporations run the only domestically licensed online gambling, and they do not generally operate affiliate programs in the commercial sense. Affiliate content aimed at those provinces therefore tends to promote offshore operators, which sit outside provincial oversight entirely. That is the part of the landscape where reader caution matters most, because no provincial regulator is supervising either the operator or the marketing.

What good affiliate practice looks like

Regulation sets a floor. The things that actually make a comparison site useful go beyond it, and they are visible to any reader who looks for them.

  • Disclosure that is easy to find, stating plainly that the site earns commission and how.
  • A published rating methodology explaining what is assessed and weighted, so rankings can be interrogated rather than taken on faith.
  • Coverage of drawbacks, not just features. A review with no criticism is advertising.
  • Accurate bonus terms, including playthrough, game weighting and expiry, rather than a headline figure with the conditions buried.
  • Age and responsible gambling messaging that is present and prominent rather than a legal afterthought.
  • Content that is updated when terms change, because stale bonus figures are the most common form of affiliate misinformation.

The rating methodology point is the most practical test available to a reader. If a site ranks operators but will not explain how, the ranking probably tracks commission rates. Our own framework is published in full, and the individual assessments sit in our casino and sportsbook reviews.

The tensions that remain

Three issues continue to sit unresolved in the Canadian affiliate landscape.

The first is lifetime revenue share and problem gambling. An affiliate compensated as a share of a player's losses has a financial interest that runs directly counter to that player gambling less. No disclosure regime fully resolves this; it is structural.

The second is enforcement reach. Provincial regulators have authority over licensed operators, and through them over affiliates promoting those operators. They have little practical leverage over an affiliate site promoting offshore operators to players in provinces with no competitive market.

The third is the blurring of affiliate content with editorial and social media content. A tipster account posting picks and a review site publishing rankings are subject to very different reader expectations, even when both are commercially compensated in the same way. Disclosure norms on social platforms remain weaker than on traditional review sites.

What this means for you

Read comparison content the way you would read any other commercially funded recommendation: useful, informed, and not disinterested. Check the disclosure. Check whether the methodology is published. Check whether any operator on the list is ever criticised. And verify the bonus terms on the operator's own site before you deposit, because those terms are the operator's, not the affiliate's, and they change without anyone updating the article.

Affiliate sites do real work. They aggregate licensing information, test payment flows, and explain terms that operators would rather bury. But the incentive structure is what it is, and a reader who understands it gets far more value from the content than one who does not. If you want to see the current state of the Canadian market without the ranking layer, our industry news coverage tracks the regulatory side directly.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
